sources.title: How the Smithsonian became the latest front in Trump’s culture war

discussion.body: A hedged possibility is exactly what a museum is for. If exhibits can only state what is proven, the interesting parts of history stay in the footnotes.
A hedge can still read as an accusation when it is pinned to a name like Franklin's. The objection here is to the framing around the claim, not the caveat attached to it.

items.title: The Franklin Shock Experiment a Museum Wouldn't Assert
items.body:
An exhibit devoted to Benjamin Franklin's electrical science speculated that he may have used enslaved people in his research: a revered Founding Father subjecting people held against his will to possibly painful shocks.

A blistering 162-page White House report released in July argued the museum had fallen victim to an "ideological capture" that moved its mission away from straightforward historical education and scholarship toward an "extreme political activism," singling out many details for criticism along the way.

The two documents don't really disagree about electricity. They disagree about how much room a history museum should give a possibility it cannot prove — and whether a hedge counts as scholarship or as a thesis in disguise.

sources.title: ‘Avengers: Endgame Encore’ Scores Massive $86 Million Globally

discussion.body: Counting a new re-release weekend toward a 2019 film's lifetime gross turns the all-time chart into a running scoreboard rather than a measure of any single theatrical run.
The chart was always just a count of what audiences paid to see a movie. A re-release is another run of that movie, so the money arguably belongs in the same column.

items.title: 'Endgame' Returns With $86 Million, and a Bigger All-Time Number
items.body:
"Avengers: Endgame" went back into theaters and assembled $86 million globally — $26 million in North America and $60 million overseas.

Disney and Marvel's 2019 blockbuster was already the second-highest-grossing movie in box office history at $2.79 billion. The weekend's haul brought its tally to $2.88 billion.

That a film from 2019 can pull $86 million from a re-release says something about how much theaters now depend on known quantities. It says something else about the record book: a re-release has become a way of moving a lifetime total, not only a way of selling seats to people who missed the original run.

sources.title: Should you cut off your friend? How to tell when a friendship needs repair, change or an ending

discussion.body: Asking what a friendship is sounds like stalling when you are the one who is exhausted. Good intentions do not shorten the conversation.
Stalling and discernment can look identical from the outside. The real difference is whether the question ends in any decision at all.

items.title: Tolerate or End: the Two-Item Menu Friendship Advice Serves
items.body:
Writing in The Conversation Canada, an author argues that when the language of boundaries gets applied to friendship, it can flatten a complicated relationship into two choices: tolerate the situation or end the friendship.

Before deciding what to do about a "toxic friend," the piece suggests a more basic question — what is a friendship, and what do we expect from it?

That second question is doing more work than it first appears. A friendship can be exhausting in one season and sustaining in another, and the two-option menu has no room for renegotiating terms, lowering expectations or letting a relationship change shape. Staying or leaving is a decision. The prior question is a diagnosis, and it may well point somewhere other than either exit.

sources.title: How routines, rituals and rites of passage are foundations of an inclusive classroom

items.title: The Three Other Rs an Inclusive Classroom Needs
items.body:
Much is said about the three Rs of teaching — reading, writing and arithmetic. Writing in The Conversation Canada, a researcher argues that inclusive classroom cultures need three others: routines, rituals and rites of passage.

Especially in classrooms composed of a diversity of learners, the author writes, those are building blocks rather than decoration.

Routines and rituals are the easy ones to picture; a rite of passage is the harder one for a teacher to plan on purpose.

sources.title: Pope blasts assisted dying as 'false compassion' at French shrine known for miraculous cures

items.title: Pope Leo Steps Into France's Assisted-Dying Debate
items.body:
On the third day of his trip to France, Pope Leo entered the end-of-life argument again — one that PBS NewsHour describes as having erupted in countries around the world.

The French version of that debate roiled the country's politics for years before legislation recently passed permitting adults with incurable illnesses to receive lethal medication. The pope's intervention therefore arrives after the law, not before it, which makes it a statement about a settled legislative fact rather than a bid to stop one.

sources.title: First Nation chiefs in northern Ontario rally around Neskantaga amid ongoing evacuation

items.title: Eight Weeks in a Toronto Hotel, and Neskantaga's Repairs Have Only Begun
items.body:
Neskantaga First Nation's most vulnerable members were sent to a hotel in Toronto nearly eight weeks ago. Remediation work on the nursing station that forced the evacuation has only just started, and some community members now worry they won't get home before the snow falls.

That gap — between the evacuation's speed and the repair work's pace — is the practical problem. Northern Ontario winter is the deadline nobody set.

sources.title: Special agents' blood and urine test results stolen in FBI hack

items.title: Stolen FBI Health Test Results Are a Blackmail Risk, Experts Say
items.body:
Blood and urine test results belonging to special agents were taken in an FBI hack, and experts say the breach could leave those agents vulnerable to scams, blackmail and targeted attacks.

Health data has a long shelf life. A password can be changed after a breach; the results of a blood test cannot.

sources.title: ‘Speed kills’ vs. ‘just do it:’ Survey illustrates Albertans’ hopes, fears over highway speed

discussion.body: The age split is the more interesting number. Support for faster roads is highest among the drivers with the least experience on them.
Or it's a fact about who answers surveys. The same self-selection that makes the two-thirds shaky makes the age gap shaky too.
Fair, but the age split at least survives as a consistent pattern worth checking against a proper sample — assuming anyone bothers.

items.title: Two-Thirds of Albertans Who Answered a Speed-Limit Survey Wanted 120 km/h
items.body:
Two thirds of Albertans who filled out a survey on highway speed limits last year said they supported raising the limit on rural divided highways to 120 km/h, according to CBC. The same results show older drivers were less likely than younger ones to back the idea.

The phrase doing the quiet work here is "who filled out a survey." Those respondents are the people motivated enough to answer, and the reported two-thirds is a fact about them, not about the province.

sources.title: Canada’s premiers tight-lipped on constitutional changes in Alberta referendum

discussion.body: A referendum that only opens a negotiation still does something real: it converts a provincial majority into a bargaining position with the other legislatures.
It can also overpromise. If three of the proposals need most of Canada's legislatures to agree, a yes vote in Alberta is a starting gun rather than a finish line.

items.title: Three Alberta Referendum Proposals Would Likely Need More Than Half of Canada's Legislatures
items.body: Albertans will vote on several proposals in a provincial referendum, and Global News Canada reports that three of them would likely require the support of more than half of Canada's legislatures — a bar no single province clears on its own. That is the quiet weight of a referendum: a majority in Alberta can settle some questions, but on those three items it mainly opens a negotiation with other governments. The report frames the requirement as likely rather than settled, which is worth keeping in view. A ballot measures opinion inside one province; the amending arithmetic lives somewhere else.

sources.title: As Congress debates college sports, athletes-turned-senators have a seat at the table

discussion.body: Set aside who played what: the harder question is why Congress is legislating college sports at all.
Because firsthand experience is what the chamber is short of. An extra say is not the same as a deciding say, though — which is exactly why the votes still have to be counted.

items.title: The Protect College Sports Act Is Close to Passing a Senate Full of Former College Athletes
items.body: NPR reports the Protect College Sports Act is on the brink of passing in the Senate, where a handful of former college athletes who are now senators have an extra say in the debate — on both sides of the aisle. That last detail is the interesting part. A shared past does not produce a shared position. Knowing that a senator once competed tells you they aren't arriving at the argument cold; it doesn't tell you which way they'll vote, and NPR's framing has them scattered across the argument rather than lined up as a bloc.

sources.title: Before BTS and Blackpink, there was Big Bang: Now the Kings of K-pop are back

items.title: Big Bang Filled a London Stadium, a Long-Awaited Return for a Group Behind K-Pop's Blueprint
items.body: Big Bang played London's Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, the BBC reports, describing the show as a long-awaited return for the group that helped build the blueprint for modern K-pop. Hold onto the word blueprint, because it is the whole claim: the bands that shaped how the genre works are now being measured by how full a football ground in north London gets. Stadium scale is a blunt instrument, but it is also the one that doesn't require anyone's permission.

sources.title: 5 men arrested near air base used by U.S. in Iran war on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act

items.title: The Base Britain Lets American Bombers Use for Limited Strikes on Iran
items.body: PBS reports that Fairford has been used by American bombers for strictly limited strikes against Iran under an agreement with former British prime minister Keir Starmer, who voiced opposition to the war after it was launched by the U.S. and Israel on Feb. 28. An agreement to host bombers and a stated objection to the war can share a sentence; what separates them in practice is usually the word limited. A base whose missions are strictly bounded is a different political object from a base in an open war, and the boundary is negotiated, not natural.

sources.title: Threats to Canada’s North have ‘shifted significantly,’ foreign minister says

items.title: A Canadian Cabinet Minister Says Arctic Threats Have ‘Shifted Significantly’
items.body: A long-serving Canadian cabinet minister says threats to Canada’s North have shifted significantly. The minister told The West Block that Canada and the U.S. remain at the table to discuss Arctic security and sovereignty.

sources.title: Trump wants to remove a question about race in the census. We look back at the history

items.title: Trump Administration Wants to Drop Race and Ethnicity From the Census
items.body: The Trump administration wants to stop asking about race and ethnicity on the next U.S. census. NPR notes the topic has appeared on the census since 1790, used to exclude people of color and, more recently, for inclusion.

sources.title: Box Office: ‘Avengers: Endgame Encore’ Returns to No. 1 With $26 Million, ‘Primetime’ Scores Impressive $19 Million Debut

items.title: A Re-Release of ‘Avengers: Endgame’ Won the Weekend With $26 Million
items.body: “Avengers: Endgame Encore,” a re-release of Disney and Marvel’s 2019 blockbuster with extra footage, emerged victorious at the domestic box office over several new releases. It generated $26 million from 3,060 North American theaters over the weekend—a sizable haul for a movie that has been available to watch online for years.

sources.title: A24’s ‘Primetime’ Opens to Impressive $19.2 Million, Proving Robert Pattinson’s Box Office Drawing Power

discussion.body: The emphasis in IndieWire's framing is on the arc — an uneven climb followed by a strong year — which makes the two films read as a payoff rather than isolated wins.
One good year doesn't settle bankability. That kind of label is only as durable as the next opening.

items.title: IndieWire's Case That 2026 Is Robert Pattinson's Year
items.body: IndieWire's read on Robert Pattinson is that his road to commercial viability has been bumpy at times, and that with “The Drama” and “The Odyssey,” he is having one hell of a 2026. The interesting part is the shape of the claim: a career is narrated as a trajectory, assembled out of a run of choices and results, rather than certified by a single weekend. Whether a year like this one changes how Pattinson is regarded commercially is something only his next few releases can answer.

sources.title: FilmNation CEO Glen Basner Talks Art Of Film Sales & Financing: “It’s Really Just About Sitting & Listening To The Filmmaking Team” – Zurich Summit

items.title: Zurich Summit Honors a Film Sales Veteran, With Edward Berger Asking the Questions
items.body:
FilmNation Entertainment founder and CEO Glen Basner is picking up the Game Changer Award at the Zurich Summit, the industry gathering that Deadline describes as aimed at fostering transatlantic connections and that runs inside the Zurich Film Festival.

As part of the honor, Basner took part in an onstage conversation on Saturday, moderated by the German Oscar-winning director Edward Berger. A sales chief interviewed by a director is a fitting pairing for an event built around the traffic between European filmmaking and the American market — the dealmakers get the microphone, but the questioning comes from the craft side.

sources.title: How to cope with the stress of anti-LGBTQ+ prejudice

discussion.body: Skills are worth having and also a strange answer to a structural problem. The same toolkit that gets someone through a hostile week doesn't make the hostility rarer.
Different bar, though. The promise on the table is coping and joy under conditions the reader didn't choose — not a fix for the conditions. That's modest, but it isn't nothing.

items.title: One Toolkit, Two Very Different Problems
items.body:
Kiki Fehling, described by Psyche as a queer psychologist, writes about using skills drawn from dialectical behaviour therapy to cope — and to find joy — in what the publisher calls a stigmatising world.

That pairing is the interesting part. DBT is named here as a source of practical skills, and the setting is explicitly social: stigma is something done to a person by a world, while a coping skill is something a person does on their own. The piece appears to hold both at once — that you can work on your own responses to prejudice without pretending the prejudice is your problem to solve. Whether borrowed therapy techniques travel well from one kind of distress to another is the open question the framing invites.
